title: Person-centered profiles at work: useful patterns without turning statistical classes into fixed types

documents.text:
# Person-centered profiles at work: useful patterns without turning statistical classes into fixed types

Narrative review draft (v2, full-text appraised) · not submission-ready · 9 October 2026

## Review question

When do organizational profiles add useful information beyond continuous dimensions, and how stable are they?

Focus confirmed by the author on 9 October 2026 ([decisions](question-decisions.md)).

## Evidence base and method

The author's folder (`Paper 13 Oct 2024/References/123POPC`) holds 33 PDFs. Thirty-one were identified against Crossref, and none is retracted. Fourteen were excluded (`screening.json`):

- **Six are "profiles" in name only.** They report no person-centred analysis: the Career Decision-Making Profiles questionnaire is a set of dimensions (screening records 3–5), and others are composite case descriptions or gender comparisons. This misnomer matters for the question. A literature search on "profiles" retrieves many studies that never form profiles.
- Five apply person-centred methods to students or clinical samples.
- Three are off-topic or unidentifiable.

The **19 included studies** apply latent profile, latent transition or cluster analysis to work-related variables. Each was searched in full text for eight analytic elements, and every hit was checked by hand (`elements.py`, `audit.json`). Hits that were only recommendations for future research or statements of others' work were discarded.

## What the collection shows

### 1. Profile enumeration is reported routinely; the case for profiles is not

Almost all included studies use fit indices (BIC, likelihood-ratio tests, entropy) to choose the number of profiles, and most report profile sizes. Four state that they also required theoretical conformity [R1, R2, R3, R4]. One such statement: "We required that the profiles identified have substantive meaning and conform with theory, as without these characteristics, the statistical artefacts might have a better fit" [R3, PDF p5]. Two others favoured parsimony [R5, R6].

The question's first half asks *when profiles add information beyond the continuous dimensions*. **No included study formally tests that.** Several assert that variable-centred approaches have limitations [R7, R8, R9], but none compares the predictive or explanatory value of profile membership against the dimensions themselves. One study applies both approaches side by side ("complementary variable- and person-centered approaches") [R2, abstract]. Its main conclusion is about the dimensions: a "general factor representing self-determination" was "the most influential factor in an employee’s motivation profile" [R2, abstract].

### 2. Profiles that differ only in level add little

The collection shows when profiles risk being continuous scores in disguise:

- Career-adaptability profiles "differed in level (i.e., low career adaptability, average career adaptability and high career adaptability), but not in shape" [R10, PDF p1].
- Across 14 Korean samples, commitment profiles reduced to "two or three profiles (i.e. fully committed, weakly committed and/or moderately committed)" [R11, abstract].

When profiles are ordered by level, a single continuous score carries most of the information.

Profiles are more informative when they differ in **shape**. One study found "six distinct commit­ ment profiles differing quantitatively and qualitatively from one another and defined by employees’ global and target-specific levels of commitment" [R4, abstract]. Separating a *global* level from *target-specific* deviations, a bifactor logic used in five included studies [R12, R2, R4, R8, R6], is the main technique in this collection for keeping profiles from simply restating overall level.

### 3. Stability is tested in a minority, and it depends on the profile and the interval

Five studies follow profiles over time [R13, R2, R10, R4, R14], and two test similarity across samples [R1, R12]:

- **Four months:** motivation profiles "were found to be highly stable over the 4-month duration of this study" [R2, abstract].
- **Three waves one month apart:** six profiles "were replicated across the three mea­ surement points", with membership "moderately to highly stable over time but also demonstrated some malleability" [R4, abstract].
- **Two years:** membership in two empowerment profiles was highly stable (79.1% to 83.2%), but other profiles were "relatively un- stable (19.7% to 20.4% for the Low Empowerment and High Information profiles)" [R14, PDF p1].
- **Twelve weekly measures:** fit experiences formed five "fit and misfit types" defined by average, variance and frequency of change [R13, abstract]. Here the profile describes a *pattern over time*, not a fixed type.
- **Across countries:** "Four very similar motivation profiles were found across samples" [R1, abstract].

Stability is therefore an empirical property of each profile, not of the method. Some configurations persist for years; others change for most members.

## Conclusions this collection supports

1. **Profiles add information mainly when they differ in shape, not just level.** Level-only solutions [R11, R10] can usually be replaced by a continuous score. Global-vs-specific modelling [R4, R2] is the main safeguard against this.
2. **The "beyond continuous dimensions" claim is asserted, not tested.** No included study compares the incremental value of profile membership against the dimensions. A credible profile study should report that comparison.
3. **Profiles are not fixed types.** Stability ranges from high over months [R2] to around 20% retention over two years for some profiles [R14]. Profiles should be reported as transitional states with transition probabilities, as latent transition analysis allows.
4. **Many "profile" studies are not person-centred at all.** Six of 33 folder records use the word for questionnaire dimensions or descriptive composites.

## Limits

- Nineteen included studies from one curated folder, heavily drawn from one methodological school (several share authors). This may overstate how often best practices, such as theoretical conformity and bifactor modelling, are used across the field.
- "Not found" for an element means no matching sentence after a machine search with hand checks. Supplements were not searched.

## Proposed research direction

The companion protocol proposes a longitudinal person-centred study with a pre-registered incremental test. Profile membership must predict a later outcome beyond the continuous global and specific scores, and transition probabilities are estimated over an interval chosen to match the expected rate of change. The protocol remains a proposal pending population, access and ethics decisions.

# Paper 13 — Empirical protocol v2: Person-centred profiles with a pre-registered incremental test

> **Status: PROPOSAL awaiting AMET University Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC) approval.** No data have been collected; no results exist. Sample sizes are computed from **assumed** smallest effects of interest, not from any study. Instruments are ScaleScope catalogue entries whose source articles were resolved on Crossref (9 October 2026). Version 2 replaces the v1 draft `paper-13-oct-2024-protocol.md`.

## 1. Research question
Do work-motivation profiles predict later engagement beyond the continuous motivation scores, and how stable is profile membership?

## 2. Hypotheses (to be pre-registered)
- H1: Profiles differ in shape, not only level, once a global factor is modelled.
- H2: Profile membership predicts T3 engagement beyond the continuous scores.
- H3: Membership stability over 6 months is below 80% for at least one profile.

## 3. Design
Three-wave survey (3 months apart) with latent profile and latent transition analysis.

**Measurement occasions**
- T1, T2 (3 months), T3 (6 months): motivation and engagement each wave

## 4. Population, eligibility and recruitment
**Population(s):** a paid online research panel (Indian working adults); working professionals in India (organisations reached through alumni, professional networks and recruiter contacts); AMET University faculty and administrative staff.

**Eligibility:** Employed adults (18+). Exclusion: failing two or more embedded attention checks; incomplete primary measures at the analysed wave (handled under §8).

**Recruitment and independence safeguards**
- **Paid online panel** — a commercial panel provider (to be selected; must allow India-resident adult workers, pre-screening on eligibility, attention checks and payment at or above the provider's fair-pay guidance). Prescreen answers are re-asked inside the survey for verification.
- **Working professionals in India** — via alumni networks, professional associations and LinkedIn posts; where organisational data (HR records, supervisor ratings) are needed, a signed **organisational access letter / data-sharing agreement** is obtained first and the organisation never sees individual responses.
- **AMET faculty and staff** — invitation sent by the study team through an institution-wide mailing list with Registrar permission, **not through line managers or HoDs**; nothing is reported at a level smaller than 5 respondents; no participation data reach appraisers.

## 5. Measures
| Construct | Instrument (ScaleScope id) | Items | Occasion | Source article (Crossref-verified) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Multidimensional work motivation | Multidimensional Work Motivation Scale (MWMS, #96) | 19 | every wave | [10.1080/1359432x.2013.877892](https://doi.org/10.1080/1359432x.2013.877892) | confirm permission/licence with copyright holder |
| Work engagement | Utrecht Work Engagement Scale (UWES-9, #2) | 9 | every wave | [10.1177/0013164405282471](https://doi.org/10.1177/0013164405282471) | confirm permission/licence with copyright holder |

All instruments are administered in English (the working language of the target population). Any translation or wording adaptation (e.g. day-level or target-shifted versions) is labelled **adapted — not validated**, piloted with cognitive interviews (n ≈ 10) and checked for factor structure before the main study.

## 6. Sample size
So that a profile holding 10% of the sample has ≈50 members: **500** completers at every wave. With assumed attrition/exclusion of 35% across waves, recruit **770**. *Assumption:* Sized so the smallest expected profile (10%) has about 50 members; confirm by simulation from pilot data.

Target completers: **500**; recruitment target: **770**. Power will be re-checked by simulation with pilot variances before pre-registration; if the target is not reachable, the study is reported as estimation (confidence intervals) rather than as a confirmatory test.

## 7. Procedure and timing
1. IEC approval → OSF pre-registration (hypotheses, analysis, exclusions, stopping rule) → pilot (n ≈ 30, not analysed for hypotheses).
2. Recruitment window ≈ 6 weeks per wave; two reminders per wave; reminders stop on withdrawal.
3. Waves linked by a self-generated pseudonymous code; the linking key is stored separately from responses.
4. Data collection ends when the recruitment target is met or the pre-registered end date passes, whichever is first.

## 8. Analysis plan
Bifactor-ESEM measurement, LPA with fit + interpretability criteria, LTA for transitions, incremental prediction vs continuous scores.

- **Missing data:** full-information maximum likelihood (or multiple imputation, 20+ imputations) under MAR; attrition analysed against baseline variables and reported.
- **Measurement:** CFA for each multi-item measure; reliability (ω and α) reported; measurement invariance across waves/groups before comparing means or paths.
- **Inference:** two-sided α = .05; effect sizes with 95% CIs; Holm correction across the confirmatory hypothesis family; exploratory analyses labelled as such.
- **Common-method bias:** temporal separation and, where planned, other-source ratings; a marker variable is included in the survey.

## 9. Ethics (ICMR 2017 National Ethical Guidelines)
- **Risk category:** Minimal risk — request **expedited review**. Rationale: Questions about everyday work experiences; no deception, no intervention, no identifiable data published.
- **Consent:** written/electronic informed consent before any question; separate consent items for each optional element (record linkage, co-worker/supervisor contact, follow-up waves).
- **Voluntariness:** no penalty for non-participation or withdrawal; no data from or to supervisors/appraisers at individual level.
- **Confidentiality & data protection:** pseudonymised data, linking key held only by the PI on an encrypted drive; processing consistent with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; retention 5 years after publication (or as the IEC directs), then deletion.
- **Support:** debrief page with the national tele-mental-health helpline (Tele-MANAS, 14416 — verify before use) and contact details of the PI and IEC.
- Ethics pack (IEC application summary, participant information sheet, consent form, debrief): `../ethics/paper-13-oct-2024-ethics-pack.md`.

## 10. Open science
OSF pre-registration before data collection; de-identified data and analysis code shared on OSF after publication where consent permits (HR-record and organisational data excluded unless the organisation agrees).

## 11. Approvals and readiness checklist
- [ ] Instrument items obtained
- [ ] Instrument permissions/licences obtained

- [ ] Panel provider selected and costed (if panel used)

## B. Participant information sheet
**Study:** Person-centred profiles with a pre-registered incremental test

**Why are we doing this study?** Our research question is: Do work-motivation profiles predict later engagement beyond the continuous motivation scores, and how stable is profile membership?

**What will I be asked to do?** Complete online questionnaires (about 15–20 minutes per survey) on 1 occasion(s) as described: T1, T2 (3 months), T3 (6 months): motivation and engagement each wave.

**Do I have to take part?** No. Taking part is voluntary. You can stop at any time and withdraw your answers up to the point the data are anonymised for analysis [date], without giving a reason and without any effect on your job, appraisal or relationship with your organisation.

**Risks:** We do not expect any risk beyond everyday life. You can skip any question.

**Benefits:** No direct benefit; a summary of findings will be offered.

**Confidentiality:** Your answers are linked across surveys by a code you create, not by your name. Your supervisor or organisation will never see your individual answers. Results are reported only for groups of 5 or more.

**Contacts:** PI [name, e-mail, phone]; AMET University IEC Member Secretary [name, e-mail, phone]. Support: Tele-MANAS national helpline 14416 (verify before use).
